When we finally reached the summit, the view of the crater lake was breathtaking. Unfortunately, on the way down, it started pouring, and we got soaked. But we ended up laughing the whole way, and that night we had black pork, which tasted even better after such a long day.

question: Tell me about a memorable trip you took in your country. Where did you go, who were you with, and what happened that made it so memorable?
rationale: 배경(과거완료)·사건·문제 해결·교훈·현재까지의 변화를 응집력 있는 문단으로 엮고, 시제와 어휘를 정밀하게 통제함.
answer_text: The most memorable trip I've taken in Korea was a three-day trip to Jeju Island last summer with my parents and my younger sister. What made it special was that we hadn't traveled together as a family in about five years, since my sister and I had both been busy with school and my parents with work. On the first day, we took it easy at Hyeopjae Beach, where the water was so clear that you could see tiny fish darting around your ankles. The real adventure, though, came on the second day, when we decided to climb Hallasan. About halfway up, my dad's knee started acting up, so instead of turning back, we slowed our pace, shared the snacks we had packed, and took turns carrying his backpack. When we finally made it to the summit, the view of the crater lake was absolutely breathtaking. Of course, on the way down, it began pouring and we got soaked to the bone, but rather than complaining, we couldn't stop laughing. Looking back, it wasn't the scenery that made the trip unforgettable. It was the fact that we worked through a tough day together, and ever since then, we've tried to take a family trip at least once a year.

[Q] How are cafes today different from the cafes you went to a few years ago? Compare the atmosphere, menus, and the way people use them.
[A·IH] Cafes have changed quite a bit over the last few years. When I was in high school, most cafes in my neighborhood were small, franchise places that all looked pretty much the same, and the menu was basically coffee with a few muffins. These days, cafes have become much more about the experience. Many of them have a unique concept, like a greenhouse theme or a minimalist gallery look, and I think that's largely because of social media, since people want to post photos of trendy places. The menus have also become way more diverse. You can find everything from croffles to vegan desserts and seasonal drinks. Another big difference is how people use cafes. Back then, they were mostly places to hang out and chat, but now they've become study spaces and offices for a lot of people. Sometimes it's hard to even find a seat because everyone is working on their laptop.

question: What kind of movies do you like to watch? Tell me about your favorite genre and why you enjoy it.
rationale: 과거 습관·현재 선호·구체적 회상을 정밀하게 연결하고, 반론 인정(That said)과 자신의 입장으로 응집된 결론을 완성함.
answer_text: My go-to genre has always been action movies. I think it goes back to when I was a kid and my dad would take me to see superhero films on Saturday mornings, which became a kind of father-son tradition. What draws me to action movies is the sheer adrenaline. Even when a film runs well over two hours, I never find myself checking my phone, because the pacing keeps me on the edge of my seat. One of my all-time favorites is the Mission Impossible series. I genuinely respect the fact that Tom Cruise performs most of his own stunts, since it gives the scenes a raw, realistic quality that CGI just can't match. I still remember watching him cling to the side of a plane as it took off and realizing I had been holding my breath the entire time. That said, I know a lot of people find action movies shallow, and to be fair, some of them do have pretty predictable plots. But for me, they're not really about the story. They're about escaping for a couple of hours, and that's exactly why I keep going back to the theater whenever a new one comes out.

answer_text: In Korea, recycling is a big part of everyday life, and the rules are pretty strict. Most households separate their trash into plastic, paper, cans, glass, and vinyl, and food waste goes into its own container. A security guard usually stands nearby, and if you put something in the wrong bin, he'll politely tell you to fix it. I've gotten into the habit of rinsing plastic containers and peeling off the labels, since contaminated plastic just ends up in the landfill. On top of that, general trash has to go in special bags that you buy, so the more you recycle, the less you pay. When my Canadian friend visited, she couldn't believe how detailed the system was.

question: Tell me about how people recycle in your country. What do people usually recycle, and how do they do it?
rationale: 제도·개인 습관·원인(종량제)·과거와의 변화·자신의 평가까지 응집된 문단으로 완결하며 시제와 어휘가 정밀함.
answer_text: In Korea, recycling has become a natural part of everyday life, and honestly, the system is a lot more detailed than in many other countries. Most households sort their waste into plastic, paper, cans, glass, and vinyl, while food scraps go into a separate container that's collected by weight. In my apartment complex, recycling day falls on Wednesday evenings, so you'll see neighbors carrying bags down to the parking lot, where there are large bins clearly labeled for each category. There's usually a security guard keeping an eye on things, and if you toss something in the wrong bin, he'll gently remind you to sort it properly. Personally, I've gotten into the habit of rinsing containers and peeling off labels, because I learned that contaminated plastic ends up in a landfill anyway. What really drives this behavior is the pay-as-you-throw system. Since general trash has to go into bags you purchase, recycling literally saves you money. When I was a kid, people were far less careful, but as the rules tightened, recycling gradually became second nature. I think it's a good example of how policy can actually change people's habits.

question: Technology has changed the way people live. What is one piece of technology that people commonly use these days, and what concerns do people have about it?
rationale: 이슈 정의·다층적 우려·원인·사회적 대응·자신의 논증을 응집된 문단으로 완결하며 양보·결과 표현을 정밀하게 사용함.
answer_text: I'd say the smartphone is the one piece of technology that has reshaped daily life more than anything else. Nowadays, we rely on it for nearly everything, whether it's banking, shopping, navigating, or simply staying in touch. However, as convenient as it is, it has also raised some serious concerns. The most obvious one is dependency. If you look around on the subway, almost everyone is glued to a screen, and casual conversations between strangers have nearly disappeared. Parents are particularly worried about children, since kids are spending hours scrolling through short-form videos, which experts say can weaken their ability to concentrate on longer tasks. Privacy is another growing issue. Many apps quietly collect location data and personal information, and after a series of large data breaches in Korea, people have become much more aware of how vulnerable that information is. In response, the government has tightened regulations, and phone makers have added features like screen time limits. Personally, I don't think the problem is the technology itself. It's more about how we choose to use it, so I believe digital literacy education is the most realistic long-term solution.

My classes start at nine, so ideally I'd like to come in around six thirty. If you don't open that early, I might have to come in the evenings instead, so I'd also like to know how crowded it usually gets after work. Another thing I'm interested in is group classes. Do you run yoga or spinning sessions, and are those included in the membership or charged separately? And finally, is there a free trial day? I'd love to come in and check out the facilities before making a decision. Great, thanks so much. I'll stop by on Saturday then.

At the transfer station, I still had to find the correct platform in a building I had never visited. I asked a staff member to confirm the connection and kept the interviewer's phone number ready in case another delay occurred. The interviewer appreciated the advance notice, even though I ultimately reached the office on time. Since that experience, I have made a habit of checking not only departure times but also station notices and alternative routes before important trips.

It used to be a quiet residential area with family-owned stores, but a new subway exit opened a few years ago, and that brought more visitors and businesses. The change has been convenient for me. I can now get groceries on my way home and meet friends without traveling downtown. At the same time, some long-standing shops have closed because rents went up, and the streets feel less familiar. Last year, a bakery that my family used to visit closed suddenly, and many neighbors were disappointed. When the bakery announced it was closing, several residents left messages thanking the owner for years of friendly service. That moment made the changes feel personal rather than just economic. My parents are pleased about the new transport links, but they also miss knowing every shopkeeper by name. I understand why the area is developing, but I hope it can keep some of its local character.

answer_text: The biggest change in my neighborhood has been the area around the subway station. When I was younger, it was mostly quiet streets lined with small family-run shops. About four years ago, the city opened a new exit and improved the sidewalks, which made the area much easier to reach. New cafés, restaurants, and apartment buildings soon followed. Those changes have made everyday life more convenient, but they have also created problems that residents did not anticipate. For instance, when a popular restaurant opened beside an old residential street, delivery motorcycles began blocking the sidewalk. Several neighbors contacted the district office, and the restaurant eventually agreed to create a separate pickup area. The situation improved, though the neighborhood is still busier than it once was. Looking ahead, I hope future development will include practical measures to protect pedestrians and support long-established businesses. The district organized a meeting after complaints about deliveries and parking began to increase. Residents asked for clearer loading zones, and a few businesses agreed to adjust their delivery times. The changes were small, but they showed that new development and neighborhood needs do not always have to be treated as opposites. I welcome the new facilities, but I would rather see the area become more livable than simply more crowded.

Fortunately, the child moved back in time, but the incident showed how risky the layout had become. Several residents contacted the district office, which promised to review the road, although no construction date has been announced. In the short term, I would suggest setting up a designated drop-off area and using crossing guards during arrival hours. If a new crossing cannot be funded immediately, temporary signs and stricter parking enforcement would still help. Over the longer term, a raised crosswalk and a redesigned corner could protect pedestrians without closing the road. I support practical changes that make the street safer before a more serious accident occurs.

answer_text: About a year ago, I decided to learn the guitar as a way to unwind after long days at university. I had always enjoyed listening to acoustic music, but I had assumed playing it would come naturally. It did not. When my friend first taught me a few chords, I struggled to change between them without losing the rhythm, and my fingertips were sore for days. I considered giving up until he helped me break one song into smaller sections and practice each transition slowly. I also started recording short clips every weekend so I could hear my progress. Over time, the changes became smoother, and I finally managed to play the entire song for a few friends. I had originally assumed that practicing longer would solve every problem, but the recordings showed that I was repeating the same mistakes. Instead, I began working on one short section at a time and checking the rhythm before increasing the speed. I still have a lot to learn, but I now understand how to practice more efficiently. I still make mistakes, but now I understand that steady practice matters more than trying to sound impressive immediately.

answer_text: Last spring, I organized a riverside picnic for five friends, and a sudden storm forced us to change our plans at the last minute. We had chosen the location a week earlier, divided up the food, and checked the forecast the night before. Unfortunately, a weather warning was issued just as people were preparing to leave. Because the river path can become slippery in heavy rain, I decided it would be irresponsible to continue with the outdoor plan. I called everyone, explained the situation, and suggested two alternatives: postponing the picnic or meeting indoors. One friend offered her apartment, which was large enough for the group, so we chose that option. I rearranged the food pickup and sent everyone the new address. We spent the afternoon eating and playing games, and the event was a success despite the inconvenience. One guest was traveling from another city, and I did not want her to arrive without knowing where to go. I called her directly, explained that the riverside area had been closed because of the storm, and arranged to meet her near the subway exit. We divided the remaining food among the group and planned to try the outdoor picnic again when the weather improved. Since then, whenever I organize something outdoors, I prepare a backup location in advance.

When the depot called, I confirmed the contents before traveling there, so I would not make another unnecessary journey. Since then, I have kept my most important cards in a separate holder and regularly checked that my bag is closed.

answer_text: During summer vacation, I volunteered at a community center that offered reading activities for elementary school students. My main responsibility was to support small groups as they worked through short English stories. I had assumed that explaining unfamiliar words would be the hardest part, but I quickly realized that several children understood the material and were simply reluctant to speak in front of others. When one student repeatedly refused to read aloud, I changed the activity: we took turns reading individual lines, acted out the characters, and gradually increased the length of each turn. By the end of the program, he was volunteering to read entire paragraphs. I also discussed the change with the program coordinator so we could use a similar approach with other students. I had initially planned to work through a fixed number of pages, but that approach left some children behind. After discussing the problem with the program coordinator, I changed the sessions to include shared reading, picture clues, and short individual turns. The adjustment made the group more comfortable and helped the quieter students participate at their own pace. The experience showed me that patience and flexibility are often more effective than correcting every error immediately.

For me, convenience matters, but being able to make an informed decision matters even more.

Two teammates prepared overlapping background slides, while the section explaining our findings had barely been started. When we discovered the problem two days before the presentation, several members became frustrated, and the discussion began to focus on who was responsible. I suggested that we first list every unfinished task and estimate how long each one would take. We then reassigned responsibilities according to each person’s strengths, set a shared deadline for drafts, and scheduled a final review meeting. I took charge of integrating the slides and checking that our explanations followed a consistent argument. We finished on time and received positive feedback, although the last two days were unnecessarily stressful. We also set a time after which no one would make independent edits to the final file. That prevented the confusion we had experienced with multiple versions. Before presenting, we rehearsed the transitions between speakers and checked that the graphs supported our conclusions. For our next project, we created a task board and agreed to flag delays early, which helped us avoid the same problem.

answer_text: I am broadly in favor of building a cultural center, provided that the city treats it as a long-term community service rather than a prestigious construction project. At present, many residents have to travel across town to attend inexpensive art classes or small performances, so a local facility could make cultural activities more accessible. However, I share concerns about the initial cost, ongoing maintenance, and the possibility that a large new building could remain underused. I would therefore recommend starting with a public consultation and publishing a clear operating plan that explains who will use the facility, how programs will be funded, and what fees residents would pay. If the budget proves too restrictive, the city could renovate an existing building and expand it gradually instead. I would also prioritize public transportation access and spaces that local organizations can reserve. My priority would be flexible rooms that different age groups can use throughout the week, rather than a large auditorium that sits empty most days. The city could begin with a few pilot classes in an existing public building and use attendance data to decide whether expansion is justified. That approach would reduce financial risk while still meeting residents’ immediate needs. With those safeguards, the project could become a genuine community resource rather than an expensive symbol.

I hope future changes will focus as much on reliable service and accessibility as on digital convenience.

I also wanted to ask: can the tickets be exchanged if one of us cannot attend? If the middle section is sold out, which nearby section would you recommend? Before we finish, could you send the seating map and final price by email before I pay? Once I check the view with my friend, I can complete the purchase today. Thank you for walking me through the choices.

These changes have not made every day perfect, but they are practical enough that I can keep returning to them. Next semester, I want to protect that consistency instead of relying on short bursts of motivation.

answer_text: one experience that stands uh out happened recently I traveled to taipei with a friend during winter break we stopped at a busy a busy train station to buy tickets for the airport I had expected everything to go smoothly but after buying the tickets I realized my small shoulder bag was missing for a moment I was unsure what to do especially because the situation affected other people as well I decided to act instead of waiting I retraced my steps and asked the information desk whether anyone had handed it in in the end a station employee found the bag near a ticket machine with um everything still inside I was frightened because my passport was in the bag and then extremely grateful looking back I realized that I mean important documents should be kept in a secure secure pocket rather than rather than a loose bag on my next trip I will use a pouch that stays close to uh my body

answer_text: The clearest way to compare them is to look at what they share and what changes in daily life. Both places are enjoyable for walking, taking photos, and watching the waves. The main difference is that urban beaches are convenient but crowded, whereas remote beaches are peaceful but harder to reach. At a beach near the city, I can find restaurants and public transportation easily. At a quieter beach, I usually see fewer buildings and hear more natural sounds. I noticed this personally: one summer, I walked along a busy promenade one day and visited an almost empty cove the next. That experience helped me see one benefit: each place suits a different kind of trip. On the other hand, isolated beaches may have fewer lifeguards or facilities. Considering those trade-offs, I choose a city beach with friends and a quiet one when I want to rest. I will check facilities and safety information before visiting a remote beach again.

Clear examples of permitted and prohibited uses would help both teachers and students.

answer_text: I think visitors and local authorities both have a responsibility to protect natural attractions, although it is not a problem with a single easy answer. To begin with, even small amounts of litter can accumulate in places that receive many visitors. At a beach cleanup event, volunteers collected plastic cups and food containers left near a walking path. Another factor is that visitors need clear information about waste disposal and areas that should not be entered. Marked trails can keep people away from fragile plants while still allowing them to enjoy the scenery. On the other hand, some travelers say that stricter rules make vacations less convenient, so I would avoid claiming that one rule will solve everything. A practical way forward is this: tourist sites should provide useful facilities and explain the reasons for the rules. That approach would address the immediate problem while leaving room for different circumstances. Ultimately, protecting a destination is part of making it enjoyable for future visitors. I would like to see more refill stations and clearly labeled collection points near major attractions.

answer_text: I think young renters need clearer housing information as well as more affordable options, although it is not a problem with a single easy answer. To begin with, advertised rent does not always show the full monthly cost. A student might choose a studio based on the rent and discover extra maintenance fees during the contract discussion. Another factor is that first-time renters may not understand which repairs are the landlord’s responsibility. A plain-language checklist could help people ask about deposits, heating, and building conditions before signing. On the other hand, property owners also face maintenance costs and cannot simply lower every price, so I would avoid claiming that one rule will solve everything. A practical way forward is this: local agencies could offer standardized cost summaries and accessible contract guidance. That approach would address the immediate problem while leaving room for different circumstances. Ultimately, transparent information would reduce avoidable disputes even if it cannot solve every housing shortage. I would like universities to offer practical housing workshops for students moving away from home.

answer_text: A few months ago, I went to see a new film with my classmates. The theater was almost full, and we had been looking forward to the final scene. I had expected everything to go smoothly, but the screen froze while the sound continued to play. For a moment I was unsure what to do, especially because the situation affected other people as well. I decided to act instead of waiting: I notified an employee, who stopped the screening and arranged for the projection system to be restarted. In the end, the film resumed from the correct scene, and the theater gave the audience a discount coupon. The interruption was frustrating, but the staff responded calmly. Afterward, I learned that reporting a technical problem clearly can help everyone. I will speak to an employee immediately if the same thing happens again.

answer_text: The clearest way to compare them is to look at what they share and what changes in daily life. Both options provide a meal without visiting a restaurant. The main difference is that home cooking takes preparation while delivery is usually quicker to arrange. Cooking at home allows me to choose ingredients and adjust the seasoning. In contrast, ordering delivery saves time when I am busy or tired. I noticed this personally: I cook pasta on weekends, but I ordered delivery before a late study session last week. That experience helped me see one benefit: having both options makes meals more flexible. On the other hand, delivery fees add up, while cooking means shopping and washing dishes. Considering those trade-offs, I cook when time allows and use delivery for particularly busy evenings. I hope to prepare simple ingredients ahead of time so I order less often.

A practical way forward is this: schools should teach practical sharing rules and choose services that explain their data practices clearly. That approach would address the immediate problem while leaving room for different circumstances. Ultimately, small habits such as reviewing permissions can prevent avoidable problems. I hope privacy training becomes a standard part of digital orientation.

answer_text: I think cities should provide reliable late-night transport on major routes, although it is not a problem with a single easy answer. To begin with, people who work evening shifts still need affordable ways to get home. Hospital employees and restaurant staff may finish after regular buses have stopped. Another factor is that clear schedules and safe waiting areas can make travel less stressful. I once waited a long time at an unfamiliar stop because the last-bus information was unclear. On the other hand, running buses late at night costs money when passenger numbers are low, so I would avoid claiming that one rule will solve everything. A practical way forward is this: cities could begin with a limited number of well-used routes and adjust service based on demand. That approach would address the immediate problem while leaving room for different circumstances. Ultimately, a carefully planned night service can support both workers and other residents. I would like transit apps to show last departures and service alerts clearly.

[Q] Have you ever returned to a neighborhood you knew when you were younger? Describe what happened during your visit, what had changed, and how you felt.
[A·IM3] Last summer, I revisited the neighborhood where I spent most of elementary school. I went with a childhood friend and hoped to see our old playground. However, the playground had been replaced by a new community center and I could barely recognize the street. At first, I didn't know how we would handle it. Then we walked around the blocks, compared old photos, and asked a shop owner about the changes. As a result, we found our old bakery still open and spent an hour talking there. I felt nostalgic even though many improvements were useful. I realized that familiar places can change while personal memories remain.

Afterward, I realized that familiar places can change while personal memories remain. I would like to visit again with more old photographs to show my family.

answer_text: Last autumn, I was shopping at a traditional market when two visitors asked me for help. They wanted to buy a local snack but could not understand the handwritten menu. I had expected everything to go smoothly, but the stall owner was busy and the visitors were unsure whether the food contained meat. For a moment I was unsure what to do, especially because the situation affected other people as well. I decided to act instead of waiting: I translated the main ingredients and helped them ask the owner a short follow-up question. In the end, they chose a snack they were comfortable eating and thanked us. I was pleased that a simple conversation made their visit easier. Afterward, I learned to confirm details with the seller rather than guess. I would gladly help again and plan to learn more useful market vocabulary.

answer_text: I believe museums should give teenagers more chances to explore exhibits actively instead of only reading descriptions, although the issue is not simple. To begin with, interactive activities help visitors connect an object with their own experiences. A hands-on science demonstration can make a difficult idea easier to remember than a long label. Another factor is that students are more engaged when they can choose topics that match their interests. A short audio tour with different routes could let teenagers select art, technology, or history exhibits. On the other hand, developing interactive displays can be expensive and staff may worry about damage, so I would avoid claiming that one rule will solve everything. A practical way forward is this: museums could start with low-cost guided challenges, student feedback, and supervised demonstration areas. That approach would address the immediate problem while leaving room for different circumstances. Ultimately, a good museum visit should encourage curiosity rather than simply require visitors to memorize facts. I hope more museums invite young people to help design educational activities.

answer_text: My view is that schools should teach practical life skills alongside traditional academic subjects. One reason is that young adults often make financial and housing decisions before they understand the details. A student renting a room for the first time may not realize that maintenance fees are separate from the advertised rent. Another factor is that simple lessons about everyday documents and responsibilities can prevent avoidable mistakes. A class could teach students to compare phone plans, read a basic contract, and make a monthly budget. Of course, school schedules are already crowded and teachers cannot cover every life situation. That is why I think schools could offer short workshops or integrate practical examples into existing subjects.

answer_text: In my view, schools should teach practical life skills alongside traditional academic subjects. There are several practical concerns to consider. To begin with, young adults often make financial and housing decisions before they understand the details. A student renting a room for the first time may not realize that maintenance fees are separate from the advertised rent. Another factor is that simple lessons about everyday documents and responsibilities can prevent avoidable mistakes. A class could teach students to compare phone plans, read a basic contract, and make a monthly budget. On the other hand, school schedules are already crowded and teachers cannot cover every life situation, so I would avoid claiming that one rule will solve everything. A practical way forward is this: schools could offer short workshops or integrate practical examples into existing subjects. That approach would address the immediate problem while leaving room for different circumstances. Ultimately, basic knowledge helps students apply what they learn to real choices. I would like universities to make reliable introductory resources available to new students.
